investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for diagnosing achalasia?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.back: Oesophageal manometry, which shows absent peristalsis together with a hypertensive lower oesophageal sphincter that fails to relax on swallowing.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.front: List the three main indications for oesophageal manometry.
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.back:
• 1) Non-obstructive dysphagia with a structurally normal endoscopy
  • 2) suspected primary motility disorder (especially achalasia)
  • and 3) mandatory work-up before anti-reflux (fundoplication) surgery.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.front: What manometric pattern suggests scleroderma (systemic sclerosis) oesophagus?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.back: Weak or absent peristalsis in the smooth-muscle oesophagus combined with a hypotensive lower oesophageal sphincter, predisposing to severe reflux.

A pressure-sensing catheter is passed transnasally into the stomach in an awake, unsedated patient, then withdrawn to straddle the LOS; a series of timed wet swallows (~5 mL water) is recorded, and HRM output is read using the Chicago Classification.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.front: What is pseudoachalasia and why must endoscopy precede manometry?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.back: Pseudoachalasia is a tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction that mimics achalasia manometrically. Endoscopy must be done first to exclude malignancy or mechanical obstruction, particularly with new dysphagia and weight loss.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.front: Achalasia is confirmed on manometry — what are the definitive treatment options?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.back: Pneumatic (balloon) dilatation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy (± partial fundoplication) or POEM. Botulinum toxin injection is reserved for patients unfit for these.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.front: Give the management of distal oesophageal spasm and of scleroderma oesophagus.
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.back:
• DES → smooth-muscle relaxants (calcium-channel blocker or nitrate) + reassurance
  • Scleroderma oesophagus (absent contractility + hypotensive LOS) → aggressive high-dose PPI; fundoplication is high-risk with such poor peristalsis.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.front: A patient has dysphagia — how do you route among endoscopy, pH study and manometry?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.back:
• Structure/mucosa (stricture, tumour, oesophagitis) → endoscopy first
  • reflux quantification → 24h pH/impedance
  • motility (achalasia, spasm) → manometry.
Manometry does not diagnose reflux or cancer.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.front: Where is the pH electrode positioned in 24-hour pH monitoring?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.back: Approximately 5 cm above the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS), which is first localised by oesophageal manometry.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.front: What acid exposure time (pH < 4) indicates pathological reflux / GORD?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.back: An acid exposure time greater than about 4–6% of the study is pathological; a DeMeester score above 14.7 is also abnormal.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.front: What does adding multichannel intraluminal impedance detect beyond pH alone?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.back:
• Non-acid and weakly-acidic reflux
  • gas reflux
  • and the direction/extent of bolus movement
  • plus symptom correlation with all reflux types.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.front: How does a Bravo capsule differ from a catheter study?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.back: It is a wireless pH capsule clipped to the oesophageal mucosa at endoscopy, allowing catheter-free recording over 48–96 hours with better patient tolerance.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.front: What does a normal pH study with ongoing symptoms and no reflux correlation suggest?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.back: Functional heartburn rather than GORD; this argues against anti-reflux surgery, which will not relieve non-reflux symptoms.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.front: Normal acid exposure time — how do functional heartburn and reflux hypersensitivity differ, and how are they managed?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.back:
Both have normal AET.
  • Reflux hypersensitivity = symptoms coincide with physiological reflux (positive symptom index/SAP)
  • functional heartburn = no symptom–reflux link.
Manage with reassurance and a neuromodulator (low-dose amitriptyline/SSRI), NOT more acid suppression or surgery.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.front: Which pH/impedance findings predict a good fundoplication outcome?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.back: Pathological AET / DeMeester + a positive symptom index + a prior symptom response to PPI. Operating on a normal study or PPI non-responders gives poor results.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: What is faecal calprotectin and why is it raised in gut inflammation?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back: It is a calcium/zinc-binding protein forming the bulk of neutrophil cytosol. When neutrophils infiltrate an inflamed intestinal mucosa they release it into the stool, where it is stable, making it a sensitive marker of active intestinal inflammation.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: What is the main clinical indication for faecal calprotectin?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back: A NICE-endorsed triage test to distinguish IBD from IBS in adults with chronic lower-GI symptoms and NO alarm features, deciding who needs colonoscopy versus who can be managed as functional (IBS).

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: Give the approximate calprotectin cut-offs and their interpretation.
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back:
• <50 micrograms/g = inflammation unlikely, supports IBS (avoid colonoscopy)
  • ~50–150 = borderline, repeat and correlate
  • >150–250 = inflammation likely, refer for colonoscopy to investigate IBD.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: Name four non-IBD causes of a raised faecal calprotectin.
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back:
• NSAIDs (enteropathy)
  • GI infection/gastroenteritis
  • coeliac disease
  • and colorectal cancer.
Calprotectin is sensitive but not specific, so a high level needs endoscopic confirmation.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: When should a patient with bowel symptoms bypass calprotectin and go straight to colonoscopy?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back:
When alarm features are present:
  • weight loss
  • PR bleeding
  • iron-deficiency anaemia
  • age >50
  • or a family history of bowel cancer/IBD.
These mandate direct referral regardless of the calprotectin result.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: How is faecal calprotectin used in a patient with KNOWN IBD?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back: To monitor disease activity, assess mucosal healing (treat-to-target), predict relapse in remission, and judge response to steroids/biologics — a falling level after induction indicates a responder.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: How does faecal calprotectin differ from FIT?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back:
• Calprotectin = neutrophil protein → marker of mucosal inflammation (IBD vs IBS), NOT a cancer test
  • FIT = detects human haemoglobin → occult bleeding / colorectal-cancer risk.
Different marker, different pathway.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: What does the Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) detect, and how?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back: It detects occult human blood in stool using an antibody specific to the globin protein of human haemoglobin. The result is quantitative, reported in micrograms of Hb per gram of faeces (µg Hb/g).

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: Why does FIT, unlike the old guaiac test (gFOBT), require no dietary preparation?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back: FIT uses a human-globin-specific antibody, so it does not react with dietary animal blood or plant/vegetable peroxidases. Patients therefore do not need to restrict red meat, vegetables or vitamin C before testing.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: What FIT threshold triggers urgent colorectal cancer referral in a symptomatic patient?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back: A FIT result of ≥10 µg Hb/g. Such patients should be referred on the urgent suspected-cancer (2-week-wait) pathway for colonoscopy.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: Does a negative FIT exclude colorectal cancer?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back: No. FIT stratifies risk but does not rule out cancer. Patients with strong red flags (rectal mass, unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia) must be referred regardless of a negative FIT.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: Why is FIT relatively insensitive to upper-GI bleeding?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back: The globin protein from upper-GI (stomach/small bowel) bleeding is digested during intestinal transit, so it is not detected. FIT therefore preferentially detects lower-GI (colorectal) bleeding.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: What FIT threshold is used in NHS bowel-cancer screening, and how does it differ from the symptomatic threshold?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back:
• Screening (England, ages 50–74, 2-yearly): ≥120 µg Hb/g → colonoscopy
  • Symptomatic (NICE NG12/DG56): ≥10 µg Hb/g → urgent 2-week-wait referral.
Screening uses a higher cut-off to balance detection against colonoscopy capacity in a low-prevalence, asymptomatic population.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.front: In two-step C. difficile testing, what does the GDH assay detect and how specific is it?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.back: GDH (glutamate dehydrogenase) is an enzyme produced by ALL C. difficile strains, toxigenic or not. It is a highly sensitive SCREEN for the organism's presence but is non-specific for disease, so it cannot distinguish infection from colonisation.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.front: How is a GDH-positive, toxin-positive stool result interpreted and managed?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.back:
This confirms active C. difficile infection.
  • Stop the precipitating antibiotic if possible
  • isolate the patient
  • and treat with oral vancomycin first-line (or fidaxomicin).

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.front: What does a GDH-positive, toxin-negative result mean?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.back: It is ambiguous: the patient may be a carrier/colonised or have early/low-toxin disease. Interpret with the clinical picture (bowel frequency, inflammatory markers); a NAAT/PCR for the toxin gene can help clarify.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.front: Which stool samples are acceptable for C. difficile testing, and why should you not test for cure?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.back: Only liquid/unformed (diarrhoeal) stool should be tested. Do not re-test to confirm cure because toxin and GDH can persist for weeks after clinical recovery, giving misleading positives.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.front: Which features signal severe/fulminant C. difficile colitis needing urgent surgical review?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.back: Rising WCC, rising lactate, abdominal distension, and ileus suggest severe/fulminant colitis with toxic megacolon. This mandates urgent senior and surgical review. Pseudomembranous colitis is the classic underlying picture.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.front: How is recurrent C. difficile infection managed?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.back:
• Fidaxomicin for a first recurrence
  • consider faecal microbiota transplant (FMT) for multiple or refractory recurrences.
(Oral vancomycin remains first-line for the initial episode.)

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.front: What are the key infection-control measures for C. difficile?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.back:
• Side-room isolation
  • contact precautions (gloves/apron)
  • hand-washing with soap and water (alcohol gel does NOT kill spores)
  • and chlorine-based environmental cleaning.
CDI is under mandatory surveillance.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.front: Why can a positive C. difficile PCR/NAAT not confirm active infection on its own?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.back: PCR detects the toxin gene, not the toxin itself. Colonised carriers are gene-positive, so a positive PCR must be interpreted with the toxin EIA and clinical picture — this is why the UK uses a two-step algorithm.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: What does faecal elastase-1 measure and why is it a reliable marker?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back: It measures a pancreatic enzyme that is stable through gut transit and not degraded, so its stool concentration reflects pancreatic exocrine output. A single random stool sample is sufficient.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: Faecal elastase cut-offs for exocrine function?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back:
• >200 micrograms/g = normal
  • 100–200 = mild-moderate insufficiency
  • <100 = severe pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: Do pancreatic enzyme supplements (Creon/PERT) need to be stopped before a faecal elastase test?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back: No. The assay is human-specific and does not cross-react with porcine-derived PERT, so supplements can be continued.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: How is confirmed pancreatic exocrine insufficiency with steatorrhoea managed?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back: Start pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (Creon) taken with meals, plus replacement of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: Key pitfall of faecal elastase and required next step?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back: A watery/loose stool dilutes the sample and can give a falsely low result. It also does not identify the cause, so image the pancreas (CT/MRI) for chronic pancreatitis or malignancy.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: What dietary advice is correct in pancreatic exocrine insufficiency?
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back: Do NOT fat-restrict. Maintain adequate fat and calories and take PERT (Creon) with every meal and snack, plus fat-soluble vitamins A/D/E/K. Fat restriction worsens malnutrition.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.front: List the causes of PEI and the key red flag on finding a new low elastase.
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.back:
Causes:
  • chronic pancreatitis (commonest)
  • cystic fibrosis
  • pancreatic cancer
  • pancreatic resection
  • coeliac disease
  • advanced diabetes.
Red flag: a new low elastase in an older patient with weight loss → exclude pancreatic cancer (CT/MRCP/EUS).

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.question: A 48-year-old with progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids has a normal endoscopy. Manometry shows absent peristalsis and a lower oesophageal sphincter that fails to relax on swallowing with raised resting pressure. What is the diagnosis?
options: Diffuse oesophageal spasm
Ineffective oesophageal motility
Achalasia
Normal study
Systemic sclerosis oesophagus
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.explanation: The combination of absent peristalsis with a hypertensive, non-relaxing LOS is the defining manometric picture of achalasia. Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset is characteristic. Barium swallow typically shows a birds-beak tapering.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.question: Before which surgical procedure is oesophageal manometry considered a mandatory part of the work-up?
options: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Elective total hip replacement
Inguinal hernia repair
Anti-reflux fundoplication surgery
Emergency appendicectomy
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.explanation: Manometry is required before fundoplication to exclude achalasia or a severe motility disorder that would be worsened by a wrap. It also confirms adequate peristaltic reserve and helps site the pH probe accurately.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.question: A 70-year-old presents with a 3-month history of dysphagia and 8 kg weight loss. Manometry appears to show an achalasia-like pattern. What is the most important next step in reasoning?
options: Repeat manometry in 12 months
Reassure and discharge as benign achalasia
Proceed directly to pneumatic dilatation
Ensure endoscopy has excluded a gastro-oesophageal junction tumour (pseudoachalasia)
Start high-dose calcium-channel blockers immediately
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.answer: Ensure endoscopy has excluded a gastro-oesophageal junction tumour (pseudoachalasia)
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.explanation: Short history, older age and marked weight loss are red flags for pseudoachalasia caused by a malignancy at the gastro-oesophageal junction. Endoscopy must exclude a tumour before attributing the picture to primary achalasia. Treating as benign achalasia risks missing a cancer.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.question: Manometry confirms achalasia in a fit 48-year-old. Which is an appropriate definitive treatment?
options: A course of broad-spectrum antibiotics
Reassurance and discharge
A calcium-channel blocker to cure the disease
Lifelong high-dose proton-pump inhibitor
Pneumatic (balloon) dilatation
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__O.explanation: Achalasia is treated by disrupting the non-relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter: pneumatic dilatation, Heller myotomy or POEM (botulinum toxin if unfit). PPIs treat acid, not the sphincter; CCBs give only weak, temporary relief and are not curative.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.question: A patient with typical heartburn but normal endoscopy is referred for 24-hour pH monitoring to confirm GORD before considering surgery. To confirm whether pathological acid reflux exists, how should the study be timed relative to PPI therapy?
options: On a doubled PPI dose throughout the study
Off PPI therapy, stopped about 7 days beforehand
Immediately after a single PPI dose on the morning of testing
PPI timing makes no difference to interpretation
On the patient's usual PPI, unchanged
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.answer: Off PPI therapy, stopped about 7 days beforehand
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.explanation: To establish whether GORD exists, acid suppression must be withdrawn so that true acid exposure can be measured. PPIs are typically stopped around 7 days before the study. Testing on therapy is reserved for assessing treatment failure, not for confirming the diagnosis.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.question: A 24-hour pH-impedance study shows an acid exposure time of 2% with a normal DeMeester score, but the patient's heartburn episodes consistently coincide with non-acid reflux events on impedance. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Severe erosive GORD requiring urgent surgery
Achalasia of the lower oesophageal sphincter
Pathological acid reflux confirming classic GORD
A technically failed study requiring repeat testing
Non-acid (weakly-acidic) reflux causing symptoms
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.explanation: The acid exposure time and DeMeester score are normal, so acid reflux is not the problem. Impedance detects the non-acid reflux events, and their consistent coincidence with symptoms identifies weakly-acidic reflux as the cause. This is exactly the scenario pH monitoring alone would miss.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.question: Which single parameter is the core quantitative measure of acid reflux burden in a 24-hour pH study?
options: Total number of swallows recorded
Gastric emptying half-time
Lower oesophageal sphincter resting pressure
Number of transient LOS relaxations per hour
Acid exposure time (percentage of study with pH < 4)
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.answer: Acid exposure time (percentage of study with pH < 4)
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.explanation: Acid exposure time, the proportion of the recording with oesophageal pH below 4, is the fundamental measure of acid reflux burden. A value above roughly 4–6% is pathological. Sphincter pressures and relaxations are manometric measures, not pH-study outputs.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.question: A patient with heartburn unresponsive to PPI has a pH/impedance study OFF PPI showing normal acid exposure time and no correlation between symptoms and reflux episodes. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Long-term twice-daily H2 antagonist
Double the proton-pump inhibitor dose
Refer for laparoscopic fundoplication
Reassurance and a low-dose neuromodulator (e.g. amitriptyline)
Urgent endoscopic mucosal resection
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.answer: Reassurance and a low-dose neuromodulator (e.g. amitriptyline)
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__2.explanation: Normal AET with no symptom–reflux association is functional heartburn. It is managed with reassurance and a neuromodulator (low-dose TCA or SSRI); escalating acid suppression or operating is inappropriate because there is no pathological reflux to treat.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.question: A 24-year-old with 3 months of loose stool and cramping, no weight loss or PR bleeding, has a faecal calprotectin of 22 micrograms/g. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The result confirms a diagnosis of Crohn's disease
The result supports IBS and colonoscopy can usually be avoided
The test must be repeated because this value is borderline
Significant intestinal inflammation is likely; refer urgently for colonoscopy
The result indicates colorectal cancer until proven otherwise
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.answer: The result supports IBS and colonoscopy can usually be avoided
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.explanation: A calprotectin below 50 micrograms/g indicates significant intestinal inflammation is unlikely. In a young patient without alarm features this supports a functional diagnosis of IBS and spares an unnecessary colonoscopy.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.question: Which statement best describes the specificity of faecal calprotectin?
options: A normal value reliably excludes colorectal cancer
It is sensitive but non-specific and is also raised by NSAIDs, infection, coeliac disease and colorectal cancer
It is specific for IBD and confirms the diagnosis when raised
It is unaffected by NSAID use
It is raised only in ulcerative colitis, not Crohn's disease
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.answer: It is sensitive but non-specific and is also raised by NSAIDs, infection, coeliac disease and colorectal cancer
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.explanation: Calprotectin reflects neutrophilic inflammation from any cause, so a raised level is non-specific. NSAIDs, gastroenteritis, coeliac disease and colorectal cancer all elevate it, which is why a high result needs endoscopic confirmation before diagnosing IBD.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.question: A 58-year-old presents with several weeks of altered bowel habit, PR bleeding and unintentional weight loss. What is the most appropriate management regarding faecal calprotectin?
options: Repeat calprotectin twice before deciding on referral
Use a normal calprotectin to safely exclude the need for further investigation
Start an NSAID and recheck the calprotectin
Refer directly for colonoscopy regardless of any calprotectin result
Reassure and treat as IBS if calprotectin is normal
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.answer: Refer directly for colonoscopy regardless of any calprotectin result
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.explanation: Alarm features such as PR bleeding, weight loss and age over 50 mandate direct referral for colonoscopy. Calprotectin is a triage test only for patients without red flags, so it must not be used to delay or avoid investigation here.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.question: A patient with established Crohn’s disease in clinical remission has a faecal calprotectin that has risen from 40 to 600 µg/g. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Definite irritable bowel syndrome
A normal, reassuring result
Coeliac disease
A new colorectal cancer
Subclinical mucosal inflammation / impending relapse
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.explanation: In known IBD a rising calprotectin reflects returning mucosal inflammation and predicts relapse, prompting review of therapy — often before symptoms return. It is not specific for cancer, and this magnitude of rise is not consistent with IBS or a normal result.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.question: A 62-year-old man reports a 3-month change in bowel habit with no visible rectal bleeding. His GP requests a FIT, which returns 24 µg Hb/g. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Refer on the urgent suspected-cancer (2-week-wait) pathway for colonoscopy
Arrange an upper-GI endoscopy
Prescribe a trial of oral iron and review in 3 months
Reassure and repeat FIT in 2 years
Advise a red-meat-free diet and repeat the test
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.answer: Refer on the urgent suspected-cancer (2-week-wait) pathway for colonoscopy
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.explanation: A symptomatic patient with a FIT of ≥10 µg Hb/g meets the threshold for urgent referral. At 24 µg Hb/g this patient should be referred on the 2-week-wait pathway for colonoscopy to investigate for colorectal cancer.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.question: Which feature distinguishes the modern Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) from the older guaiac faecal occult blood test (gFOBT)?
options: FIT preferentially detects upper-GI bleeding
FIT relies on a peroxidase colour-change reaction
FIT is a purely qualitative positive-or-negative result
FIT detects human haemoglobin specifically and needs no dietary restriction
FIT requires the patient to avoid red meat and vitamin C beforehand
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.answer: FIT detects human haemoglobin specifically and needs no dietary restriction
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.explanation: FIT uses an antibody against human globin, so it does not react with dietary animal blood or plant peroxidases and requires no dietary preparation. It is also quantitative, reporting the haemoglobin concentration in µg Hb/g.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.question: A 70-year-old woman has unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia and a palpable rectal mass. Her FIT returns as negative (below threshold). What is the correct interpretation and action?
options: The negative FIT excludes colorectal cancer, so reassure her
Refer urgently for colonoscopy despite the negative FIT, given the red-flag features
Repeat the FIT before taking any further action
Switch to a guaiac test as it is more sensitive
The mass is confirmed benign because there is no occult bleeding
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.answer: Refer urgently for colonoscopy despite the negative FIT, given the red-flag features
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.explanation: A negative FIT does not exclude colorectal cancer; it stratifies risk rather than ruling out disease. A rectal mass with unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia is a strong red flag mandating urgent referral regardless of the FIT result.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.question: An asymptomatic 62-year-old returns a positive home FIT kit (above threshold) through the NHS bowel-cancer screening programme. What is the appropriate next step?
options: No action as she is asymptomatic
Start a proton-pump inhibitor
Reassurance and repeat FIT in 2 years
Colonoscopy
Faecal calprotectin
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.explanation: A positive screening FIT (≥120 µg Hb/g in England) is followed by colonoscopy to look for colorectal cancer or adenomas. Repeating in 2 years or reassurance would inappropriately delay diagnosis; calprotectin assesses inflammation, not cancer risk.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.question: A 74-year-old inpatient develops profuse watery diarrhoea 6 days after starting co-amoxiclav. Stool testing returns GDH positive and toxin A/B positive. What is the most appropriate first-line management?
options: Start intravenous metronidazole and repeat stool testing daily
Stop the precipitating antibiotic and start oral vancomycin
Send a formed stool sample in one week to confirm cure
Reassure and continue current antibiotics as this reflects colonisation only
Give a stat dose of loperamide to control the diarrhoea
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.answer: Stop the precipitating antibiotic and start oral vancomycin
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.explanation: GDH-positive with toxin-positive confirms active C. difficile infection. First-line management is to stop the precipitating antibiotic where possible and give oral vancomycin. Antimotility agents such as loperamide are avoided as they can precipitate toxic megacolon.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.question: A stool sample from a patient with diarrhoea returns GDH positive but toxin A/B negative. How should this result be interpreted?
options: Definite C. difficile infection requiring immediate treatment
Diagnostic of pseudomembranous colitis on its own
Laboratory error requiring a repeat GDH screen only
Potential carrier or early/low-toxin disease; interpret clinically and consider PCR
C. difficile completely excluded, so no further action
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.answer: Potential carrier or early/low-toxin disease; interpret clinically and consider PCR
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.explanation: GDH detects the organism but not toxin, so a GDH-positive, toxin-negative result is ambiguous. The patient may be a carrier or have early/low-toxin disease, and the result must be interpreted with the clinical picture. A NAAT/PCR for the toxin gene can help clarify.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.question: Which stool specimen is appropriate to submit for two-step C. difficile testing?
options: Any stool regardless of consistency to maximise sensitivity
A formed stool from an asymptomatic contact for screening
A formed, well-shaped stool to confirm eradication after treatment
A liquid, unformed stool that takes the shape of its container
A rectal swab taken during digital examination
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.answer: A liquid, unformed stool that takes the shape of its container
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.explanation: Only liquid or unformed diarrhoeal stool should be tested, as a positive result on formed stool reflects colonisation rather than infection. Testing formed stool or re-testing for cure leads to over-treatment because toxin can persist after recovery.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.question: A patient successfully treated for C. difficile infection returns two weeks later with a further episode of confirmed CDI. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: No antibiotics — this is expected
Loperamide to control the diarrhoea
IV metronidazole alone
A further identical course of the same first-line agent
Fidaxomicin
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C.explanation: For a first recurrence of CDI, fidaxomicin is preferred; multiple/refractory recurrences are an indication for faecal microbiota transplant. Antimotility agents such as loperamide are avoided as they risk toxic megacolon.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.question: A 52-year-old man with a history of alcohol excess presents with weight loss and pale, greasy, offensive stools. Which faecal elastase-1 value indicates severe pancreatic exocrine insufficiency?
options: <100 micrograms/g
>200 micrograms/g
Exactly 200 micrograms/g
150 micrograms/g
Any detectable level
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.explanation: A faecal elastase-1 below 100 micrograms/g defines severe pancreatic exocrine insufficiency. Values of 100–200 indicate mild-moderate insufficiency, and above 200 is normal.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.question: A patient already taking Creon is due to have a faecal elastase test. What advice is correct regarding the medication?
options: Stop Creon for 7 days beforehand
Double the Creon dose before the test
Switch to a non-porcine enzyme first
Stop Creon for 24 hours beforehand
Continue Creon as normal
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.explanation: The faecal elastase assay is human-specific and does not cross-react with porcine-derived enzyme replacement. Supplements can therefore be continued without affecting the result.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.question: A faecal elastase performed on a loose, watery stool returns a low value. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Dilution may cause a falsely low result; repeat on a formed stool
It excludes pancreatic malignancy
It mandates immediate pancreatic resection
It indicates the enzyme was degraded in transit
It confirms severe pancreatic insufficiency
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.answer: Dilution may cause a falsely low result; repeat on a formed stool
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.explanation: Watery stool dilutes the sample and can produce a falsely low elastase concentration. Testing a formed stool gives a more reliable measure of exocrine function.

investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.question: A man with chronic pancreatitis has faecal elastase <100 µg/g, steatorrhoea and weight loss. Alongside pancreatic enzyme replacement, what dietary advice is correct?
options: Restrict protein intake
Maintain a normal-fat diet and dose PERT to meals
Adopt a strict low-fat diet to reduce steatorrhoea
Avoid all dietary fat and rely on carbohydrate
Fast before meals to reduce enzyme demand
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.answer: Maintain a normal-fat diet and dose PERT to meals
investigations__GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__F.explanation: PEI is treated by replacing enzymes (PERT with meals) and maintaining adequate fat and calories, not by restricting fat. Fat restriction worsens weight loss and fat-soluble-vitamin deficiency; fat-soluble vitamins A/D/E/K are also replaced.
